Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Germany Gun stash discovered in German forest believed to be linked to Russia, say reports Authorities believe handguns found in forest near Berlin were ⁠to be used ⁠to ​carry out assassinations for Russian intelligence, Sueddeutsche reports Reuters Fri 21 Aug 2026 06.13 EDT Last modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 06.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google German security authorities discovered handguns stashed in ⁠a forest near Berlin last year that they believe were ⁠to be used ⁠to ​carry out assassinations on behalf of Russian intelligence, Süddeutsche Zeitung reported on ⁠Friday. The Russian embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The ⁠newspaper’s report, published jointly with the broadcasters NDR and ​WDR on Friday, ‌cited unspecified ‌sources as saying that one suspect had been ‌arrested in Romania and may have been responsible for setting up the weapons storage. The federal public prosecutor’s office was investigating the case on suspicion of planning of a ‌serious act of violence posing a threat to the state, the report ​said. The paper said Germany’s domestic intelligence service, which has been warning of a heightened risk of Russian sabotage or assassination attempts, ⁠was convinced that those setting up the cache were ​acting ​on orders from ​Russian services. Potential targets included defence ​industry executives, exiled ‌opposition figures ​and ​supporters of Ukraine, the report said. The federal public prosecutor and Germany’s domestic intelligence service declined to comment. https://english.radio.cz/petr-novak-roma.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК Petr Novák: The romantic voice of the Prague Spring Facebook Twitter Petr Novák's unmistakeable, delicate tenor voice is synonymous with Czechoslovak society of the late 1960s. This talented musician shot to fame in this country at the time of the Prague Spring, when his gentle love songs influenced by Western pop groups like The Beatles were hugely popular among young Czechs. Petr Novák: The romantic voice of the Prague Spring 30:50 ⨯ Petr Novák: The romantic voice of the Prague Spring https://english.radio.cz/petr-novak-romantic-voice-prague-spring-8895834#player=on Copy Share on social media Facebook X Born in Prague in 1945, he grew up in a family deeply affected by the communist takeover of Czechoslovakia. His difficult childhood and strong opposition to the communist regime would remain an important part of his character throughout his life. Novák was drawn to music from an early age and began playing the piano when he was six. He never received formal musical training, however, and his education was cut short when he was expelled from grammar school shortly before graduation. Music eventually became his profession, even though he followed a very different path from traditionally trained musicians. He formed his first band with friends in the early 1960s, and the group soon attracted attention after several of their recordings were played on the radio. One of Novák’s early songs, Já budu chodit po špičkách, quickly became a major hit and established him as a prominent figure in the emerging Czech beat and pop scene. During the following years, Novák performed with several bands, including Flamengo, before returning to his own group, George & Beatovens. Most of the songs for both groups were written by Novák with his childhood friend and lyricist Ivo Plicka. They primarily specialised in wistful, Western-sounding love songs, which struck a chord with young Czechs and Slovaks enthused by the relaxed political and social atmosphere of the Prague Spring. After George & Beatovens was dissolved in the 1970s, Novák continued performing as a solo artist. He appeared at clubs, theaters and concerts across Czechoslovakia and also took part in ambitious musical projects. His career was not without serious setbacks. A major car accident in the 1970s left him badly injured, but he returned to performing. He continued to work throughout the following decades, appearing on television and on stage and recording new material. In the 1980s, he also created several thematic albums that reflected his personal experiences and interests. Behind his musical achievements, Novák struggled with serious health problems for much of his adult life. He ate very little, smoked heavily and drank alcohol, and was repeatedly hospitalized. His health was further weakened by injuries and circulation problems, yet he continued performing even when doing so became increasingly difficult. Petr Novák died in his sleep in August 1997 at the age of 51. His career was marked by remarkable creativity, personal struggles and an unmistakable musical identity. Decades after his death, his songs remain part of the Czech musical landscape and continue to be remembered by generations of listeners. https://www.travelerstoday.com/articles/.text: What Happened to Google Vacation Rentals in the EEA?Google has removed its dedicated vacation-rental search unit from Google Search results across the European Economic Area, a change that took effect September 8, 2026, and eliminates one of the few ways EEA travelers could compare and book short-term rentals directly — at no commission — without going through Airbnb, Booking.com, or Vrbo.The search giant said in an email to partners, first shared on LinkedIn, that the move is part of its ongoing compliance with the Digital Markets Act, the EU's flagship law targeting the largest digital platforms. "As part of these changes, we are not currently able to display the current vacation rentals unit on Search in the EEA, hence, we're removing this unit in the EEA," Google wrote, according to Skift's reporting on the changes.How Does Losing Google's Direct-Booking Unit Affect What Travelers Pay?The now-removed unit was not just a search filter — it was a commission-free booking gateway. When a traveler in Paris, Berlin, or Warsaw found a property through Google Vacation Rentals, they were redirected to the host's own direct booking website; Google charged the host nothing. By contrast, when that same traveler books through Airbnb or Booking.com, those platforms collect OTA fees typically running 15-20 percent. Hosts routinely pass those costs on in the form of higher nightly rates.With the dedicated Search unit gone, EEA travelers searching Google for a vacation rental will no longer see an aggregated comparison of properties with real-time availability. They will instead see organic results pointing to OTA listing pages or the platforms' own search tools — restoring those intermediaries to the center of the booking funnel for European markets.Hospitable, a property management platform that connects hosts to Google Vacation Rentals, updated its documentation on September 8 to mark the removal as permanent: "EEA-based vacation rental hosts will no longer receive impressions, clicks or bookings through GVR on Google Search — this is a permanent change by Google, not a bug or account issue," the company wrote. The vacation rental feed infrastructure itself remains intact; it will continue to power listings on Google Maps and google.com/hotels, and searches originating from outside the EEA are unaffected.What Has the DMA Forced Google to Remove From European Search?The vacation-rental unit's removal is one of the most visible steps Google has taken since the European Commission fined Alphabet €890 million on July 23, 2026 — the largest penalty yet under the Digital Markets Act and the first time the company had been sanctioned under the law. The Commission split the penalty into two decisions: €460 million for self-preferencing Google's own services in Search results, and €430 million for restricting how app developers on Google Play could direct users toward cheaper purchasing options on competing platforms.Google was given 60 days to demonstrate compliance with the search-preferencing decision, placing the hard deadline at approximately September 21, 2026. The September 8 removal of the vacation-rental unit appears to be the company acting within that window rather than waiting for it to close.The vacation-rental unit is not the only travel feature being scaled back for EEA users. According to reporting by Skift published the same day, Google also removed the ability for EEA users to filter travel results by date, view live pricing, and use descriptive tags within the accommodation search experience — features that remain fully available to travelers using Google outside the EU and EEA.What Can EEA Travelers Still Find on Google?The change removes the dedicated vacation-rental Search unit but leaves two other Google surfaces operational. Vacation rental feeds can still populate listings on Google Maps and on google.com/hotels, and those listings remain visible to EEA users searching on those platforms. Properties that were already live in Google Vacation Rentals before September 8 retain their feed connections; they simply no longer appear within the Search results carousel that had been the primary discovery surface.For travelers planning EEA stays, the practical implication is a return to platform-by-platform searching: Airbnb, VRBO, Booking.com, or direct booking sites found through organic search results. Travelers who specifically want to avoid OTA fees can search the platform or host's own website directly, but the one-stop comparison layer Google had provided is no longer part of Search.Why Aggregators Called the Removal a Win for Fair CompetitionThe change drew immediate approval from the aggregator side of the industry. Patrick Andrae, co-founder and chief executive of Berlin-based HomeToGo, one of the largest vacation rental search engines in Europe, described the removal as "a silver lining for fair competition" in a LinkedIn post cited by Skift. Commenters on the post responded approvingly.That reaction reflects the multi-year argument aggregators and online travel agencies have made to EU regulators: that Google's vacation-rental unit gave direct-booking results a structural advantage by placing them in a prominent, richly formatted Search module that comparison sites found difficult to replicate at equivalent prominence. Henna Virkkunen, the European Commission's executive vice president for tech sovereignty, security and democracy, framed the July DMA enforcement decision in similar terms: "We found that Google harms businesses offering similar services, such as shopping or sports, by not granting them the same level of prominence on Google Search," she said.Nick Fox, Google's senior vice president of knowledge and information, pushed back directly, arguing that the DMA-driven changes work against the interests of the travelers and hosts the regulations are ostensibly meant to protect. "These changes degrade the user experience for Europeans — boosting online intermediaries at the expense of local businesses, and removing helpful features people rely on every day," Fox said in a public statement. Google has argued previously that earlier DMA-related adjustments caused direct booking traffic to drop by approximately 30 percent, pushing more demand toward commission-charging OTAs — a figure the company has cited but that has not been independently verified.Will Google Bring Back Vacation Rentals in Europe?Google's own language leaves the door open. The company's partner email said it "hopes to bring back a vacation rentals experience in the EEA in the future" and pledged to keep partners informed of any changes. That language is deliberately provisional — suggesting Google views the removal as a technical compliance measure rather than a permanent product decision, and that the company intends to re-engineer the feature in a form the Commission accepts.Whether that proves possible within the DMA's constraints is unresolved. The law prohibits Google from giving its own travel tools preferential placement over comparable third-party services — and any rebuilt vacation-rental unit would need to satisfy that standard. For hosts and travelers in the EEA, the realistic near-term expectation, based on how long prior DMA negotiations have taken, is that the commission-free direct booking channel on Google Search remains unavailable for at minimum several months. The compliance deadline of approximately September 21, 2026, carries significant financial stakes: failure to satisfy the Commission's requirements within the 60-day window exposes Google to DMA periodic penalty exposure — up to 5 percent of its worldwide daily turnover.

https://www.politico.eu/article/first-po.text: PARIS — The first publicly available poll following the violence that rocked France over the weekend showed little change in voter intentions in next spring’s presidential election. While even some of far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen’s adversaries expected her to get a boost from the rioting and looting that took place on the sidelines of peaceful protests on Saturday, the survey published by Ifop and Fiducial found little change in her support levels. Nor was there much change in voting intentions toward far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, whom the government has repeatedly blamed for stoking the violence. Mélenchon and his allies have repeatedly and forcefully denied the accusation. Advertisement Advertisement The poll was conducted online from 8 p.m. Saturday — after rioting and looting had begun — until Monday. Le Pen remains well ahead of the pack with 34% to 38% of the vote in the various scenarios tested. Given France’s presidential election moves to a two-person runoff if no candidate obtains a majority of votes on the first round, the battle for second place is shaping to be the most crucial story of the election. That fight looks like it will be a tight one. Mélenchon’s position remains similar to what it was before Saturday, despite the attempt by the government and his opponents to tie him to the unrest. The Ifop Fiducial survey has him either in sole possession of second place or tied for it in the various scenarios tested, though his lead on his nearest competitors — center-right former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe and center-left MEP Raphaël Glucksmann — is in some cases within the margin of error. “The first feedback we’ve had from the ground — including from areas where we’re not held in high regard — is that the tactic of blaming us for everything isn’t working,” said a high-level Mélenchon campaign operative, granted anonymity to discuss internal campaign analysis. Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau told broadcaster TF1 on Monday that she “absolutely [could] not confirm” the government’s analysis based on the profiles of those arrested and placed under investigation in the French capital so far. Advertisement Advertisement The government, meanwhile, continues to fend off critics who allege that it has mismanaged the affair, which they are concerned could snowball into a sustained movement like the Yellow Vest demonstrations of 2018. Calls for more protests this coming Saturday have emerged online, prompting Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu to order what he called on Tuesday a “massive” police apparatus to avoid more scenes of vandalism, arson and mayhem. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said elite tactical police and a military unit normally deployed on French soil for counterterrorism operations would be mobilized as well. After localized curfews were established throughout the country Monday, Lecornu said it would be up to local and regional authorities to renew them Tuesday night.
